title: Chargeback Evidence Checklist: How to Build a Strong Dispute Response
summary: Build a chargeback evidence checklist, match documents to reason codes, understand representment and Visa CE 3.0, and use practical response examples.
body_markdown:
Table of Contents


Toggle


The customer lodges a complaint. They claim they did not receive an order, or that they had not made the payment. You now have only a few days to provide a response.


A[chargeback dispute](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-disputes/) is assessed using the applicable rules and evidence from the parties involved. To win a dispute you need strong evidence; weak or general evidence may result in losing a dispute, even if you were in fact correct. No evidence checklist guarantees a win.


Below we outline the basics of how representment works, what constitutes “compelling” evidence, a checklist of possible chargeback evidence types based on the dispute, and some practical advice on winning a chargeback dispute.


### Key Takeaways


- Match every document to the dispute reason code. Proof of delivery, purchase history and refund records answer different claims.
- Check the response deadline immediately. Our chargeback response window is generally three calendar days, with shorter windows at later stages.
- Visa CE 3.0 applies to eligible 10.4 card-absent fraud disputes and requires qualifying historical transactions and matching data.
- Submit relevant evidence early, accept valid customer claims and weigh escalation costs. No checklist guarantees a win.


##


What Does Chargeback Representment Mean?


Representment refers to the process of defending yourself against a chargeback by providing evidence that the transaction occurred correctly.[Mastercard’s merchant guidance](https://www.mastercard.com/in/en/news-and-trends/Insights/2024/how-can-merchants-dispute-credit-card-chargebacks.html) describes it as a written rebuttal supported by relevant transaction records.


For the most part, this occurs as follows. The customer disputes the transaction with their bank. The dispute reaches your payment provider through the acquiring side, which then contacts you, advising you of the customer’s reasons for disputing. You then decide to either accept the dispute (the customer receives a refund, and the dispute is closed) or contest the dispute.


You contest the dispute by submitting evidence. The issuing bank reviews your evidence. If the dispute remains unresolved, it may progress through pre-arbitration and finally arbitration, where the card network or NPCI makes a decision after reviewing evidence provided by both parties, depending on the[payment mode](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/payment-mode-types/) . Not every case passes through every stage of the[dispute process](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/manage/disputes/disputes-process-flow) .


If you fail to respond to a chargeback dispute, you automatically lose, and the customer will receive their refund under default circumstances.


Deadlines are tight. Our[dispute response timelines](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/manage/disputes/disputes-types) include the following windows:


**Stage** **Merchant response time** **Typical card timeline** **Typical UPI timeline**


Retrieval 3 calendar days 30 to 45 days waiting period, if contested Not specified


Chargeback 3 calendar days 30 to 45 days 15 to 20 days


Pre-arbitration 2 calendar days 30 to 45 days 15 to 20 days


Arbitration 1 calendar day About 15 days About 15 days


The deadlines given above are specific to our dispute workflow. Timelines may vary depending on the acquirer, card network, dispute reason code and case. Some fraud disputes require a response within one day. International card disputes may follow separate network rules. Before preparing any evidence, always confirm the response window shown in your dispute dashboard. These are response deadlines and indicative stage timelines, not a guaranteed overall resolution time.


##


What Constitutes Compelling Evidence in a Chargeback?


Visa defines compelling evidence as showing that the card holder was involved in the transaction, received the goods or services associated with the transaction or benefited from them.


**Evidence could be:**


- Proof that the cardholder is utilizing the product/service.
- Previous undisputed transactions.
- Emails from the cardholder stating that they have received their purchase or requesting help on how to utilize/activate the item.


Compelling evidence does not guarantee a win for you; however, it provides the issuer with information to assess the claim. The applicable card-network rules and dispute condition determine what evidence is relevant. A delivery record and a fraud defence answer different questions.


##


Chargeback Evidence Checklist: Documents to Keep Ready


Prep these docs ahead of time so you will have quick access to the necessary documentation to defend your claims. Our[reason-code and document guide](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/manage/disputes/reason-codes) includes these standard evidence types:


- Proof of delivery or service
- Shipping documents
- Statement of service
- Proof of service used
- Cancellation of service proof
- [Refund documentation](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/manage/refunds/overview)
- Business model description
- Declaration of additional fees
- Terms & Conditions
- Customer withdrawal letter (if applicable)
- Certificate of authenticity
- Reseller agreement


Not every dispute requires all of the above. The key is to submit sufficient evidence to answer the customer’s complaint. Include the order ID, payment reference, amount and relevant dates so the reviewer can connect each document to the disputed payment. Keep evidence legible and label attachments clearly. A customer withdrawal letter does not replace responding through the dispute process.


##


Match Chargeback Evidence to the Dispute Reason Code


Each chargeback case includes a reason code which identifies the basis of the customer’s claim against you. In addition to providing your evidence to refute their claim, your evidence should be directed at specifically refuting the claim identified by the reason code.


Reason codes vary depending upon the network. Below are examples found in our dispute documentation. Use the exact code and condition in your dispute notice; codes and handling can vary by programme and version.


**Dispute category** **Visa** **Mastercard examples** **RuPay and UPI examples**


Fraud 10.1 to 10.5 4837, 4840, 4849, 4870, 4871 128 for RuPay; use the stated UPI dispute code


Not received 13.1 4855 1064


Not as described, counterfeit or misrepresentation 13.3, 13.4, 13.5, depending on the claim 4853: cardholder disputes; check the specific condition 1062


Duplicate 12.6 4834: point-of-interaction error; check the specific condition 1084


Credit not processed 13.6 4860 1061


### Fraud or an Unauthorised Transaction


The customer states that they did not authorise the transaction. Provide matching details from the customer’s past orders (including device, IP address, account/email address/delivery address).


### Goods or Services Not Received


The customer states that they did not receive the merchandise. If it is a physical goods item, provide proof of delivery showing the full delivery address. If it is a digital goods item, provide download access records showing device data and/or IP address. If it is a travel or event item, provide proof that the ticket was used.


### Not as Described, Defective or Counterfeit


The customer states that the item ordered did not meet the expectations established by the description. Provide evidence of how the product was described on your website, provide evidence of your Terms & Conditions, and any relevant certificate of authenticity. Address the specific allegation: a return policy alone does not prove that an item matched its description or was genuine.


### Duplicate Transactions


The customer states that they received duplicate charges. Document and provide evidence that the charges occurred from two (2) different transactions or that an initial refund has been made to the customer. Two invoices alone may not establish two authorised purchases. Include the separate order details and delivery, enrolment or service records where relevant.


### Credit or Refund Not Processed


The customer states that they are entitled to credit/refund. Provide documentation/evidence that a credit/refund has been made to the customer; document evidence that establishes why a refund/credit should not be made to the customer. If a refund was already processed, include its amount, date, status and available bank/reference number. Check the open dispute before issuing another refund to avoid returning the amount twice.


### Cancelled Recurring Subscription


The customer states the recurring subscription was cancelled; however, they have been charged for it again. Provide your proof of cancellation (cancellation of service document), including the terms of their original subscription agreement. Reason code 13.2 is used by Visa when processing this type of dispute, therefore, be sure to review the dispute reason code prior to responding, in order to include supporting documentation which addresses that specific claim. Show the cancellation request date, when cancellation became effective, and the disputed billing date. If the customer was charged in error after cancellation, accept the valid claim.


***Also read:[Chargeback vs Refund vs Reversal: Key Differences](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/chargeback-vs-refund-vs-reversal/)***


##


Visa Compelling Evidence 3.0: When Can It Support a Fraud Defence?


Fraud claims are often difficult to defend. The Compelling Evidence 3.0 (CE 3.0) programme developed by Visa provides a defined route for eligible **10.4 card-absent fraud disputes** . It is not a general defence for every fraud, delivery or refund claim.


Before using CE 3.0, confirm all applicable requirements with your acquirer, including:


- At least two qualifying prior transactions made using the same payment credential. Visa applies specific 120-day and 365-day timing conditions, with exceptions; have your acquirer validate the relevant date calculations for your case.
- Those prior transactions were not reported as fraudulent by the issuer before the disputed transaction and meet the applicable fraud-reporting requirements.
- For both of these prior transactions and the disputed transaction in question, the required matching data points are available: customer account/ID, delivery address, device ID/fingerprint and IP address.


The usual matching requirement is at least two qualifying data elements, including device ID/fingerprint or IP address. Confirm the complete rule set for the transaction and programme.


In addition to meeting the applicable conditions, include item descriptions for the disputed and qualifying prior transactions.


If a merchant meets each of the applicable requirements, CE 3.0 may support a liability shift to the issuer. Eligibility and submission through a supported acquiring process still matter.


There is one caveat, however. Since CE 3.0 requires qualifying prior purchases, it is generally unavailable for a genuinely new customer with no eligible transaction history. Other permitted evidence may still be relevant to the dispute.


***Also read:[Friendly Fraud- Why It Happens and How to Prevent It](https://www.cashfree.com/blog/friendly-fraud/)***


##


How to Win a Chargeback Dispute: Practical Response Tips


**Respond on time:** Failure to meet the deadline will result in losing your case by default.


**Respond to the reason code:** Sending generic evidence will not likely help you win your case. It is imperative that you send evidence that directly responds to the reason code provided in the dispute notice.


**Save your data:** To assess eligibility for the Compelling Evidence programme, you will need access to qualifying historical order data. In particular, preserve relevant device and IP information along with delivery and account records under your lawful retention policy. Use payment references or permitted tokens rather than retaining raw card numbers or CVVs for evidence.


**Collect proof of delivery:** Shipping products without collecting proof of delivery could cost you money down the line.


**Do not contest everything:** Pre-arbitration and arbitration can involve significant fees or penalties under the applicable rules. If you lose a case brought before an arbitrator, the costs associated with the arbitration may fall on you. Only escalate your case if you believe you truly have evidence to support your position and understand the costs.


**Submit complete evidence early:** In our workflow, once a case reaches arbitration, no additional evidence can be uploaded. Evidence submitted during pre-arbitration is automatically carried forward. The[Contest Arbitration API](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/api-reference/payments/latest/disputes/contest-arbitration-by-dispute-id) submits the contest decision without new documents. Do not wait until pre-arbitration to supply evidence already needed for your first response.

##


Chargeback Response Examples: What to Write and Attach


Below are four illustrative chargeback response examples demonstrating how evidence can be presented in relation to the claim. They are templates, not actual case outcomes. Replace every bracketed field with verified records and omit any assertion you cannot support.


### Example 1: Order Was Not Received


A customer files a claim against an online sale of a headphone. The merchant submits evidence from the courier (the courier’s proof of delivery) identifying the full address of the customer; an order invoice; and the tracking history.


**Sample response:** “Order \[ID\] was delivered to the order address on \[date\]. Attachment A is the courier’s delivery confirmation showing \[recipient/address details\]; Attachment B is the invoice, and Attachment C is the tracking history. These records link the delivered order to payment \[reference\].”


### Example 2: Duplicate Transaction


A customer states they have been charged for the same course twice. In this case, the merchant provides two invoices that both reflect two separate transactions (with two different enrollment dates). The merchant also supplies the separate course enrolments and access records, where available.


**Sample response:** “The payments on \[date 1\] and \[date 2\] relate to separate purchases: \[order/course 1\] and \[order/course 2\]. The attached invoices, order confirmations and enrolment records show the service associated with each charge.” If there was only one purchase, do not describe a duplicate debit as a separate sale.


### Example 3: Claim of Fraud


A customer claims they did not purchase a software subscription. The merchant then presents evidence of two prior undisputed payments on the same permitted payment credential, five and eight months respectively before the disputed payment date, along with the same device ID and account login information. The acquirer must verify all CE 3.0 timing, matching and fraud-reporting conditions; this example does not establish eligibility by itself.


**Sample response:** “Payment \[reference\] relates to subscription \[ID\]. The attached records link it to account \[ID\] and device \[identifier\]. We have included qualifying prior transaction records for the acquirer’s CE 3.0 assessment, subject to the applicable Visa requirements.”


### Example 4: Item Not as Described


A customer claims a handbag purchased was counterfeit. The merchant supplies evidence of the product page viewed by the customer when making their original purchase; a certificate of authenticity; and the customer’s agreement to the terms and conditions at check-out.


**Sample response:** “The customer disputes the authenticity of product \[item/order ID\]. Attachment A is the product listing in effect on \[purchase date\]. Attachments B and C contain the manufacturer’s purchase record and authenticity documentation identifying \[model/serial details\]. These records relate to the item supplied under this order.” Checkout acceptance alone does not establish authenticity.


##


How We Help You Manage Chargeback Evidence


Our Merchant Dashboard includes an[Action Required section](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/manage/disputes/dashboard-actions) listing all disputes requiring a response. The dashboard indicates which disputes require a response by today/tomorrow and highlights those disputes where additional evidence needs to be uploaded to support your position.


You may also set up[email notifications](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/payments/manage/disputes/overview) for new disputes and updates on dispute status, use our[dispute evidence API](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/api-reference/payments/latest/disputes/submit-evidence-to-contest-the-dispute-by-dispute-id) to submit documents associated with each dispute before arbitration, and use[dispute webhooks](https://www.cashfree.com/docs/api-reference/payments/latest/disputes/dispute-webhooks) to receive notifications when a dispute is created, updated or closed. The issuer or network decides the outcome.


##


Conclusion


Chargeback evidence is strongest when it answers the claim exactly, arrives on time and is supported by data you have saved.


Before a chargeback occurs, create your evidence file. Match each piece of evidence to its specific reason codes. Escalate only those claims where you have evidence to support your position.

##


Frequently Asked Questions


#### What is chargeback evidence?


Chargeback evidence is documentation merchants provide which supports a claimed transaction was valid. Examples include; proof of delivery, an invoice, customer communications, terms and conditions, etc., as well as refund records.


#### What constitutes compelling evidence in a chargeback?


Compelling evidence according to Visa is any proof that shows the card holder participated in the transaction, received products/services or benefited from the transaction.


#### Do I lose the dispute if I do not respond to a chargeback?


Yes. If you do not respond to a chargeback, you will lose the dispute and the card holder will be refunded.


#### How long does a chargeback dispute take with Cashfree?


The total length of a dispute with Cashfree may take approximately three months, contingent upon the number of rounds involved. Use the deadline on the individual case for your response; this overall estimate is not extra time to submit evidence.


#### What does chargeback representment mean?


This means you are going to be disputing the chargeback with evidence supporting your claim of a legitimate transaction. The issuer will then review all the evidence presented and make their decision on how to proceed.


#### Can I present new evidence at arbitration?


In our dispute workflow, no new evidence can be uploaded at arbitration. All information provided at pre-arbitration is carried forward as part of the record. Confirm the applicable process with your provider if using a different arrangement.
